Vaunt
VAWNT
verb
From the Old French vanter, from the Late Latin vanitare, “to speak vainly, to boast,” from vanus, “empty, vain”; hence to boast, to brag, to display oneself — literally, to make much of emptiness.

Biblical Definition

To vaunt is to boast, to brag, to set oneself forth — and the Latin root confesses the whole indictment, for vanus is empty: to vaunt is to make much of nothing. The word governs one of the great scenes of the Old Testament. The LORD said unto Gideon, “The people that are with thee are too many for me to give the Midianites into their hands, lest Israel vaunt themselves against me, saying, Mine own hand hath saved me” (Jdg 7:2). Thirty-two thousand were too many; God pared them to three hundred with pitchers and lamps, not because He needed fewer but because Israel needed to know who saved them. Divine arithmetic is always aimed at the boast: God will win the battle in a way that leaves no room for the creature to vaunt. Paul draws the same line over salvation itself: “Not of works, lest any man should boast” (Eph 2:9). Grace is designed against vaunting; election, effectual calling, and imputed righteousness leave the sinner with nothing to display but Christ. And in the great chapter of love the word becomes a portrait: “charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up” (1Co 13:4). Charity is the exact opposite of the vaunting spirit, for love looks outward while boasting looks in the glass. Solomon shuts the door on the last excuse: “Boast not thyself of to morrow; for thou knowest not what a day may bring forth” (Pro 27:1). The man who vaunts does not even own his next hour.

Webster 1828 Definition

To boast; to brag; to make a vain display of oneself or one’s doings.

expand to see more

VAUNT, to boast; to brag; to make a vain display of what one is or has done.

From the Latin vanus, “empty” — to vaunt is to make much of nothing.

God thinned Gideon’s army lest Israel vaunt themselves against Him (Jdg 7:2).

Charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up (1Co 13:4).

Salvation is not of works, lest any man should boast (Eph 2:9).

Key Scripture

1Co 13:4 — "Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up,"

Jdg 7:2 — "And the LORD said unto Gideon, The people that are with thee are too many for me to give the Midianites into their hands, lest Israel vaunt themselves against me, saying, Mine own hand hath saved me."

Eph 2:9 — "Not of works, lest any man should boast."

Pro 27:1 — "Boast not thyself of to morrow; for thou knowest not what a day may bring forth."

Modern Corruption

A live corruption: the age has made vaunting a discipline and calls it confidence; Scripture calls it making much of emptiness.

expand to see more

Here is a corruption fully alive, and it is taught now as a skill. The self must be presented, the brand built, the accomplishment displayed; the man who does not vaunt himself is told he will be passed over. Scripture answers with the etymology: vanus is empty, and to vaunt is to make a loud noise about nothing. Charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up — love looks outward at its object, while boasting stands before the glass and admires. And Solomon strips the boaster of even his ground: boast not thyself of to morrow, for thou knowest not what a day may bring forth. The man who vaunts is bragging about property he does not own.

The doctrine underneath is grace itself. God thinned Gideon’s thirty-two thousand to three hundred for one stated reason — lest Israel vaunt themselves against Him, saying, Mine own hand hath saved me. The LORD arranges His victories so that the creature cannot claim them. So it is in salvation: not of works, lest any man should boast. Election is not of foreseen merit, the call is effectual and not earned, the righteousness is imputed and not ours; every door by which a boast might enter is shut deliberately. He that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord. The saint has everything and vaunts nothing, for he owns not one thing he did not receive.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means to boast or brag, to make a vain display of oneself.

expand to see more

Vaunt — Old French vanter, from Late Latin vanitare, “to speak vainly.”

From vanus, “empty, vain” — the boast is a noise about nothing.

It denotes bragging, the display of self and self's doings.

God spared Israel the vaunt by winning with three hundred (Jdg 7:2).

Charity vaunteth not itself; grace leaves no room to boast (1Co 13:4; Eph 2:9).

Usage

"Too many for me, said the LORD — lest Israel vaunt themselves and say, Mine own hand hath saved me."

"Charity vaunteth not itself: love looks at its object, boasting looks in the glass."

"Not of works, lest any man should boast — grace is designed against the vaunt."
